- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is positive or neutral (e.g., +0.5+ sentiment) — model tends to overshoot and fail to correct.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., -1.2+), especially if recent prices are high — model fails to recognize downward pressure.
- Lag in correction: model often delays mean reversion, especially after strong sentiment shifts — adjust forecast to reflect recent sentiment momentum.
- When sentiment is volatile or mixed, model overfits short-term noise — reduce forecast variance and favor smoother transitions.
- If sentiment is consistently positive over 3–5 days, model tends to overreact — cap upward forecasts at 1–2% above recent high.
- If sentiment is consistently negative over 3–5 days, model tends to underreact — add 1–2% downward buffer to forecast.
- Avoid forecasting sharp reversals without recent sentiment confirmation — if sentiment is neutral or mixed, don’t assume direction.
- When sentiment is high but price is flat, model often assumes continuation — instead, assume mean reversion or slight pullback.
- Forecast should not exceed 3–5% above recent 18-day high unless sentiment is strongly bullish and sustained.
- Forecast should not fall below 3–5% below recent 18-day low unless sentiment is strongly bearish and sustained.
